items.title: Some quadratics never touch zero — and you can prove it in one step
items.claim: x^2 + 2x + 5: positive for every real x. The graph never reaches zero. You don't need calculus or graph-plotting — you can see this in one rearrangement.

options.text: Complete the square: x^2 + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)^2 + 4. The first term is non-negative; adding 4 means the whole expression is at least 4. Never zero
It cannot be proved without calculus

items.reveal:
For ax^2 + bx + c with a > 0, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines:
- Discriminant > 0: two real roots; graph crosses x-axis twice.
- Discriminant = 0: one repeated real root; graph touches x-axis.
- Discriminant < 0: no real roots; graph stays entirely above x-axis (if a > 0) or below (if a < 0).

x^2 + 2x + 5: a = 1, b = 2, c = 5. Discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0. No real roots.

Completing the square gives a stronger statement: the MINIMUM value of the quadratic. (x + 1)^2 + 4 has minimum 4 when x = -1. So x^2 + 2x + 5 is always at least 4.

General quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = a(x + b/(2a))^2 + (c - b^2/(4a)). Minimum value (for a > 0) is c - b^2/(4a) = -(b^2 - 4ac)/(4a) — same expression as the discriminant.

Applications:
- Optimisation: many minimisation problems reduce to completing the square.
- Inequality proofs: AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz often pivot on quadratic positivity.
- Definite matrices: a quadratic form x^T M x > 0 for all non-zero x means M is positive definite — central to optimisation and statistics.
items.why: Quadratics feel like they should always cross zero somewhere. Many don't. The discriminant settles which ones, and completing the square exposes the minimum directly — without calculus.

items.title: Newton's method finds square roots in just a few steps
items.claim: To estimate sqrt(2): guess 1.5. Improve by averaging 1.5 with 2/1.5 = 1.333. New estimate: 1.417. Repeat with 2/1.417 = 1.412. New: 1.414. Already 4 decimals of accuracy in 2 steps from a poor start.
items.prompt: Why does this rapid convergence happen?

options.text: Newton's method converges QUADRATICALLY near a simple root: each step roughly DOUBLES the number of correct digits. 4 iterations of 10 correct digits each gives 16 digits — far faster than linear convergence
It is the only method that works on square roots
All iterative methods converge equally fast

items.reveal:
Newton-Raphson iteration: to solve f(x) = 0, iterate x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n). Geometrically: draw tangent at current point, take where it crosses the x-axis as next estimate.

For sqrt(a), solve f(x) = x^2 - a = 0. f'(x) = 2x. Iteration: x_(n+1) = x_n - (x_n^2 - a)/(2x_n) = (x_n + a/x_n)/2. This is the 'Babylonian method' — known since ~1700 BC.

Convergence rate: if x_n is the current estimate and r is the true root, |x_(n+1) - r| is roughly proportional to |x_n - r|^2. The error squares at each step — quadratic convergence. Roughly: number of correct digits doubles per iteration.

Starting from 1.5 for sqrt(2) (true value 1.41421...):
Step 1: 1.41667 (3 correct digits)
Step 2: 1.41421568 (6 correct digits)
Step 3: 1.414213562373... (12+ correct digits)
Step 4: limited only by floating-point precision.

Newton's method can also fail:
- If f'(x) = 0 nearby, division by zero or huge steps.
- For multi-root or degenerate roots, convergence is only linear.
- Bad initial guesses can cycle, diverge, or jump to a different root.

Fractal basins of attraction: for complex polynomial roots, Newton's method partitions the plane into 'basins' that have fractal boundaries. The Newton fractal is one of the prettiest objects in computational mathematics.
items.why: Iterative methods for solving equations look like trial and error. Newton-Raphson is far better — each step squares the precision, making it the workhorse of computational mathematics.

items.title: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Diagonal of a unit square has length root 2. The Pythagoreans believed all lengths were ratios of whole numbers. Hippasus showed root 2 wasn't. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned him for revealing it.
items.prompt: Sketch the proof that root 2 is irrational.

options.text: It has too many decimal places

Assume root 2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b squared = a squared, so a is even (say a = 2c). Then 2b squared = 4c squared, so b squared = 2c squared, so b is even. But a and b were lowest terms — contradiction
Because computers can't store it exactly

items.reveal:
The Pythagorean brotherhood (c. 500 BC) believed numbers were the foundation of reality and that all measurable lengths could be expressed as ratios of integers.

Hippasus of Metapontum supposedly proved the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side. Different ancient sources say he drowned at sea — some say by accident, some say murdered by his fellow Pythagoreans for exposing the result.

The proof: suppose root 2 equals a/b in lowest terms. Squaring: 2 = a squared over b squared, so 2 b squared equals a squared. Hence a squared is even, so a is even (say a = 2c). Substituting: 2 b squared = 4 c squared, so b squared = 2 c squared, so b squared is even, so b is even. Both a and b are even — contradiction with 'lowest terms'.

The discovery that not all numbers are rational was a major shock; the Greeks came to call these new quantities 'incommensurable'. Modern mathematics calls them irrationals — and there are vastly more of them than rationals.
items.why: Numbers feel like they should always be expressible as ratios. The very first geometric constructions reveal they're not.
